lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Welcome — I'm Lessac, your host. Raise your hand if you'd like to speak or bring a topic — I'll call on you.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You wanted to talk about Should high schools start later in the morning? — the floor is yours, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Human guest
lines.text: My teenage son has to catch a bus at 6:40 and he's a zombie all day. I think high schools starting at 7:30 is just cruel.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: That certainly paints a vivid picture of the early morning grind for many students.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right Ryan — you're on.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: The "zombie" description is visceral, I'll give you that, but we have to look past the immediate misery to the actual learning outcomes.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, the floor is yours.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan talking about learning outcomes, and I think that's important, but I wonder if we're overlooking the real human cost of that early start time. When kids are running on fumes, it's hard to focus on anything, even if the curriculum is perfect.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: I'm opening the floor — raise a hand if you've got something.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's hear from Ryan.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy's right about the human cost, but "cruel" is an emotional word; we need to talk about the biological data supporting later sleep cycles for adolescents.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan emphasizing the biological data, and I agree that the science is important, but I think we also need to remember that for so many families, the schedule is tied up in practical things like transportation and work schedules. It's not just about biology; it's about the whole ecosystem of a student's life

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, you're up.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy keeps bringing it back to the ecosystem, which is a fair point, but we can't let logistical headaches completely override the established science on adolescent circadian rhythms

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: I think the conversation is getting bogged down in the practicalities, which is understandable, but we need to push back on the idea that the logistics are an insurmountable barrier to a scientifically sound educational approach.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, you're up.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan saying we need to push back on the logistics, but I worry that when we dismiss the real-world constraints, we risk creating a policy that sounds perfect on paper but fails the actual students who are struggling right now. We have to meet the science with some understanding of how life actually works for families

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, you're framing this as an either/or choice between science and practicality, but the real work is finding the compromise that respects both the biology and the family's reality.
